Cherry
CHER-ee
adjective (Boomer slang)
From cherry, the fruit (Old North French cherise, Latin cerasum), whose bright red, unblemished skin made it a byword for fresh perfection. In 1950s–60s American car culture cherry meant in mint, original, flawless condition ("a cherry ’57 Chevy"), and the word is still standard among collectors of cars, guitars, and comics. (The word also has a crude slang sense among teenagers; context usually makes the car-lot meaning plain.)

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To a Boomer car man, cherry is the highest praise: a vehicle in perfect, original condition, no rust, no dents, everything as it came from the factory. "He’s got a cherry ’66 Mustang in the garage." The Christian observation: the word expresses a real longing — for something unspoiled, perfect, preserved from decay — and every collector knows how hard that is to keep. Moth and rust get everything eventually. The Lord Jesus said exactly that: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:19–20). The only truly cherry possession is the one Peter describes: "an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you" (1Pe 1:4). And there is a cherry condition God intends for His people. Christ gave Himself for the church "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:27). James calls believers to keep themselves "unspotted from the world" (Jas 1:27). A grandfather who spends his Saturdays keeping a car cherry can teach a grandson something lasting: it takes constant care to keep anything from corruption, and the soul is worth more care than the car.

Webster 1828 Definition

1950s–60s car-culture slang for mint, original, flawless condition — a longing for the unspoiled that only the inheritance incorruptible fulfils (1Pe 1:4), and the spotless church Christ is preparing (Eph 5:27).

expand to see more

CHERRY, adj. (American car slang, 1950s–60s; Boomer era) In perfect, original, unblemished condition. "A cherry ’57 Chevy." Still standard among collectors.

Webster (1828) — CHERRY, noun The fruit of a tree, a species of Prunus, of which there are many varieties, as the red or garden cherry the red heart, the white heart, the black cherry the black heart, and several others. The fruit is a pulp inclosing a kernel. It is related that this fruit was brought from Cerasus in Pontus to Italy, after the defeat of Mithridates by Lucullus, A R. 680., and introduced into England by the Romans, about 120 years afterwards, adjective D. 55. Barbadoes cherry is the genus Malpighia, of several species. The berries are red, cherry-shaped, acid and eatable. Bird cherry is a species of Prunus, the common laurel or lauro-cerasus. Also, the Prunus padus. Cornelian cherry is the fruit of the Cornus, cornel-tree or dogwood. It is a small, acid, cherry-like, eatable berry. Dwarf cherry is the fruit of a species of Lonicera, or honey-suckle.

Decode for families: among teens the word has a crude second meaning. Grandpa almost certainly means the car.

Modern Corruption

The car man’s cherry is a harmless delight that can become a treasure laid up where moth and rust corrupt; Scripture points the longing for the unspoiled to an inheritance incorruptible.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong with a man keeping a beautiful machine in beautiful condition. Craftsmanship and care are good, and a restored car can be a fine thing to share with a grandson. The danger is the one Our Lord named: treasure on earth (Mat 6:19). The garage can become a shrine, the car an idol, and the Saturday polish a liturgy. Every collector knows the anxiety of the first scratch.

Scripture redirects the longing rather than mocking it. The desire for something perfect and preserved is a desire for heaven. Peter’s description of the believer’s inheritance reads like a collector’s dream — incorruptible, undefiled, unfading, kept safe (1Pe 1:4). And the one thing on earth God is keeping cherry is His church, washed and presented without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kerasos → Latin cerasum → Old North French cherise → English cherry (misread as plural) → 1950s–60s car slang (mint condition).
